title: How Much Practice Do Students Need?
author: Fivetwelvethirteen Source: fivetwelvethirteen.substack.com
summary: An empirical approach to a classic teaching problem: students can perform a skill during class but forget it the next day. The key cognitive science distinction is between retrieval strength (how easily something is recalled right now) and storage strength (how durable that memory is over time). When students can do something in the moment but forget it overnight, they have high retrieval strength but low storage strength. The counterintuitive fix is to let them forget slightly, then practice again — each day's brief check-for-understanding followed by additional practice meaningfully builds storage strength. The author checks for understanding on day two, day three, and so on, watching the success-rate percentage climb toward 100%. Once mastery is reliable, retrieval practice (one or two questions mixed into daily Do Nows) maintains it. This approach may require redesigning instruction — either dedicating opening minutes to prior-topic review, or stretching the hardest strands across the entire school year rather than teaching them in a single unit.
points: Retrieval strength fades quickly after initial learning; storage strength develops only through spaced, repeated retrieval over multiple days — practicing ten times in a row adds far less than practicing, waiting a day, and practicing again.
The practical threshold for 'enough practice' is when students can reliably retrieve the skill the next day — not just during the lesson in which it was taught.
When the success rate reaches 80–90%, shift focus to the remaining stragglers while the class continues brief maintenance practice; at 100%, transition to full retrieval-practice mode.
The author stretched the hardest math strands across the whole year in parallel — multiple topics side by side every day — providing the time and flexibility that spaced practice requires.
Many schools insist each lesson must have exactly one objective; the author argues this is incompatible with how humans learn, since meaningful learning always spans multiple days.
quotes: Cognitive scientists delineate two different types of memory strength: retrieval strength and storage strength. When you first learn something, retrieval strength is high.
The best way to improve storage strength is counterintuitive: forget a little bit, then practice again.

Learning is a change in long-term memory, and the best practical way to measure long-term memory is to wait a day and see what students remember. Continue practicing until students reach that threshold.

Many teachers and schools are strongly committed to the idea that every lesson must have exactly one objective, and every part of the lesson must be in service of that objective. I think we should let go of that idea. It simply is not consistent with how humans learn.
I took the toughest topics, the ones that students typically have the most trouble with, and stretched them out through the entire year.
